strengths: Addresses an important problem with a practical approach: retrieving existing unlabeled nodes avoids synthesizing node features and graph neighborhoods, and the framework works across GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE.

The reported evaluation is broad, covering five datasets, imbalance ratios up to 100, naturally imbalanced settings, and five repetitions. Some gains are substantial: on CiteSeer with GCN at ratio 10, F1 improves from the strongest baseline's 56.32 to 64.94.

Pseudo-label accuracy diagnostics, component ablations, and sensitivity experiments provide useful evidence about the proposed mechanisms. The appendix supplies substantial dataset and training details.
weaknesses: Numerical inconsistencies materially weaken confidence in the evidence. In Table 8, GCN at ratio 5 reports 11,593.6 aligned and 2,308.4 discarded nodes, totaling 13,902 rather than the stated 13,632 unlabeled nodes. Table 9 reports 96.40 ± 4.27 as mean accuracy and standard error over five repetitions; five percentages averaging 96.40 cannot have a standard error exceeding 3.60. Corrected summaries and individual-run results are needed.

Originality relative to the closest prior work is insufficiently established. M3S, acknowledged in Section 6, already filters pseudo-labels through agreement between clustering and classifier predictions, closely resembling DPAM. There is no explicit M3S comparison or precise explanation of the differences. The DPAM-plus-confidence ablation provides a partial comparison, but only in four selected settings.

The ablations provide mixed support for the additional components. In Table 11, the complete method barely improves over geometric ranking alone on PubMed/GAT: 77.38 versus 77.32 F1. Removing DGIN improves CiteSeer/SAGE from 57.51 to 58.71. A comparison against a simple fixed-weight ranking combination is also missing, leaving the specific benefit of RBO weighting uncertain.

The technical description contains inconsistencies. DPAM assigns labels using cluster centroids, so a retained node's assigned class need not be its nearest class center, contrary to the premise used in Section 4.3. Appendix C.6 also reverses the threshold's effect: increasing gamma rejects more nodes under Equation (8), whereas the discussion says it introduces more noise.

Reproducibility and computational claims remain incomplete despite the extensive hyperparameter ranges. Selected configurations, the F1 averaging convention, and whether each retraining round restarts or continues training are unspecified. With 40–100 rounds and up to 2,000 epochs per round, runtime, peak-memory measurements, and matched self-training budgets are needed to establish the claimed computational advantages.

Some conclusions exceed the experimental support. Increasing the imbalance ratio from 20 to 50 or 100 also increases majority-class label counts and changes the citation-data sampling protocol, confounding conclusions about imbalance alone. Claims of consistent superiority also overlook counterexamples, including Computers-Random/GraphSAGE in Table 2. These limitations, together with the reporting errors and unresolved comparison to prior work, outweigh the promising benchmark gains.
